title: Sugar coating the invasion: how smut fungi sweet-talk maize cell wall guards
content: Plant pathogens and their hosts are engaged in a perpetual evolutionary arms race. As plants evolve increasingly sophisticated defense mechanisms to prevent infection, pathogens respond with equally ingenious strategies to circumvent them (Peng et al. 2018). The first physical barrier encountered by an invading pathogen is the plant cell wall, a dynamic extracellular structure that provides mechanical support and serves as the primary line of defense. Successful invasion depends on the pathogen's ability to breach the host cell wall (Mohnen 2008; Cosgrove 2024). Although pathogens employ an arsenal of cell wall–degrading enzymes to break down host structural components, this enzymatic breakdown releases damage-associated molecular patterns that trigger plant immune signaling, activate antimicrobial defenses, and induce growth-defense tradeoffs. How biotrophic pathogens remodel the host cell wall for colonization without triggering massive immune activation remains a central question in plant pathology.
